title: The Importance of Cross Training for Dancers
content:
Benefits of Cross Training for Dancers

Injury Prevention: Dancing puts repetitive stress on certain muscles and joints, increasing the risk of overuse injuries. Cross training helps alleviate this risk by distributing the workload across different muscle groups and reducing strain on vulnerable areas.

Improved Strength and Conditioning: Cross training activities such as strength training, yoga, and pilates build muscular strength, endurance, and stability, enhancing dancers' ability to execute movements with power and control.

Enhanced Flexibility and Range of Motion: Incorporating activities like yoga and stretching routines into your training regimen can improve flexibility and joint mobility, allowing dancers to achieve greater range of motion and fluidity in their movements.

Cardiovascular Fitness: Aerobic exercises such as swimming, cycling, or running improve cardiovascular health and stamina, vital for sustaining energy levels during prolonged dance rehearsals or performances.

Mental Refreshment: Cross training introduces variety into your workout routine, preventing boredom and burnout. Engaging in different activities stimulates the mind and provides a mental break from the intensity of dance training.




Effective Cross Training Activities

Strength Training: Focus on exercises that target major muscle groups, including squats, lunges, deadlifts, and planks. Incorporate resistance bands, free weights, or bodyweight exercises to build strength and stability.

Yoga and Pilates: These practices promote flexibility, core strength, and body awareness, essential for maintaining proper alignment and posture in dance movements.

Swimming: A low-impact cardiovascular workout that improves endurance and promotes full-body strength and coordination.

Cycling or Spinning: Builds leg strength, cardiovascular fitness, and stamina while minimizing impact on the joints.

Interval Training: Alternating between periods of high-intensity activity and rest improves aerobic capacity and endurance, simulating the dynamic nature of dance.

Cross training is a valuable complement to dance practice, offering numerous benefits that enhance performance and reduce the risk of injury. By incorporating a variety of activities into your training routine, you can develop a strong, resilient body capable of meeting the physical demands of dance while maintaining overall health and well-being.
description: Dance is a physically demanding art form that requires strength, flexibility, endurance, and agility. While regular dance practice is essential for improving technique and mastering choreography, cross training plays a crucial role in enhancing overall performance and preventing injuries.

title: The Do's and Don'ts of Contacting a Collegiate Dance Team Coach
content:
The Don'ts

1. Don’t DM Their Personal Account

Why It’s Important: Coaches maintain a professional boundary between their personal and professional lives. Direct messaging their personal accounts can come off as intrusive and unprofessional unless they explicitly state otherwise.

Alternative: Use official channels such as the coach’s professional email or the team’s contact form. This ensures your communication is both formal and respectful.

2. Don’t Send an Introductory Email Without a Highlight Reel or Resume

Why It’s Important: Coaches receive numerous emails from potential recruits. Providing a highlight reel or resume helps them quickly assess your skills and determine if you’re a good fit for their program.

Alternative: Send them a link to your Studio 2 Stadium profile so all information is organized in one place and make sure your recent highlight videos are up to date.This demonstrates preparedness and seriousness about joining their team.

3. Don’t Have Your Parents Email Them

Why It’s Important: Coaches want to see that you are taking responsibility for your journey. Having your parents email them can give the impression that you’re not mature enough to handle the communication yourself.

Alternative: Take the initiative to email the coach yourself. It shows maturity, independence, and genuine interest in their program.

4. Don’t Contact Them Without Doing Research First

Why It’s Important: Coaches’ time is valuable. Reaching out without knowing basic information about the program can waste their time and reflect poorly on your preparation.

Alternative: Research the team, its achievements, coaching style, and what they look for in recruits. Tailor your email to reflect this knowledge and show that you’re truly interested in their program.

5. Don’t Text or Call Them Late at Night

Why It’s Important: Coaches have lives outside of their professional responsibilities. Contacting them late at night can be seen as disrespectful and intrusive.

Alternative: Reach out during normal business hours. If you’re unsure when that is, a safe window is typically between 9 AM and 5 PM on weekdays.

6. Don’t Speak Poorly About Other Schools or Programs

Why It’s Important: The dance community is small and interconnected. Negative comments can travel quickly and harm your reputation.

Alternative: Focus on the positive aspects of the program you’re interested in and your goals. Maintaining a positive and professional tone is key.

7. Don’t Accept an Interview If You’ve Been Rejected Academically

Why It’s Important: Coaches invest time and resources in recruits who are eligible to join their institution. If you’ve been rejected academically, continuing the recruitment process wastes both your time and theirs.

Alternative: Ensure you meet the academic requirements before pursuing a spot on the team. If you’re rejected academically, consider other schools where you meet the criteria.

8. Don’t Ask for Their Personal Email or Phone Number

Why It’s Important: Privacy and boundaries are important to maintain a professional relationship. Asking for personal contact information can make the coach uncomfortable.

Alternative: Stick to the contact information provided officially. If the coach offers personal contact details, it should be on their own terms.

The Do's

1. Do Email Them During the Off Season

Why It’s Important: The off-season is a less hectic time for coaches, allowing them to review your materials thoroughly and respond more promptly. Since it is their off season don't expect a reply straight away and wait at least a month before reaching back out. Coaches need vacation time too!

How to Do It: Craft a well-thought-out email introducing yourself, attaching your resume, and including a link to your S2S profile. Mention your interest in their program and why you think you’d be a good fit.

2. Do Ask to Set Up a Call or In-Person Meeting

Why It’s Important: Building a relationship with the coach can significantly impact your chances. Personal interactions allow you to learn more about the program and make a stronger impression.

How to Do It: After your initial email, follow up with a request for a phone call or meeting. Express your eagerness to discuss the program further and learn more about their expectations.

3. Do Have Questions Prepared

Why It’s Important: Coaches often ask if you have any questions at the end of a meeting. Being prepared shows your interest and diligence.

What to Ask: Inquire about the team’s culture, expectations for recruits, and opportunities for growth. Thoughtful questions can demonstrate your commitment and curiosity.

4. Do Thank Them for Their Time

Why It’s Important: Coaches often go out of their way to meet with recruits without additional compensation. Showing appreciation for their time is courteous and leaves a positive impression.

How to Do It: Send a thank-you email after your meeting, expressing gratitude for their time and reiterating your interest in the program.

5. Do Be Honest with Them

Why It’s Important: Transparency about your goals and other universities you are considering helps build trust. Coaches appreciate honesty and clear communication.

How to Do It: In your communications, be upfront about your aspirations, other programs you’re looking at, and any potential obstacles. Honest conversations can lead to better guidance and support from the coach.

Personal Thoughts and Experiences

From my experience I’ve seen firsthand how following these do’s and don’ts can impact a recruit’s journey. Coaches appreciate candidates who show respect, preparedness, and genuine interest. It’s not just about your dance skills but also how you present yourself as a responsible and mature individual.

For example, when I was recruiting one of my prospects made the mistake of having their parent handle all communications with me. Despite being a talented dancer, this lack of personal accountability negatively affected my perception. On the other hand, another dancer I recruited took the time to research the program thoroughly, personalized their communications, and followed up diligently. She is still currently dancing at the collegiate level and is very successful.

In conclusion, approaching the recruitment process with professionalism, respect, and preparedness can significantly enhance your chances of success. Coaches are looking for talented dancers who are also reliable, mature, and genuinely interested in their program. By following these guidelines, you can make a positive impression and set the stage for a successful collegiate dance career.

title: Delegating Tasks: Fostering Team Involvement and Reducing Workload
content:
In the dynamic world of dance coaching, it's not uncommon for coaches to find themselves juggling numerous responsibilities. From choreography planning to administrative tasks, to second jobs, the workload can quickly become overwhelming. However, one effective strategy for managing this workload while fostering a sense of team involvement is delegating tasks to dancers.

Delegation involves entrusting specific tasks or responsibilities to members of your team. By distributing tasks among dancers, you not only alleviate some of the workload on your shoulders but also empower your team members to take ownership and contribute to the collective success of the group. Additionally, delegating tasks can provide valuable learning opportunities for dancers to develop new skills and enhance their sense of responsibility.

Assigning Roles and Responsibilities

When delegating tasks to dancers, it's essential to consider each individual's strengths, interests, and availability. Assigning roles and responsibilities that align with their skills and preferences can increase motivation and engagement. Here are some examples of tasks that can be delegated to dancers:

Choreography Assistance: Assign dancers to collaborate with you in creating choreography for routines. This not only lightens your workload but also fosters creativity and collaboration within the team.

Rhinestoning Team: As is widely recognized, the process of rhinestoning is both time-consuming and requires meticulous attention to detail. Delegating this responsibility to dancers who excel in this task not only saves valuable time but also provides a calming and enjoyable activity for those who appreciate it.

Leadership Roles: Identify dancers who demonstrate strong leadership skills and appoint them as team captains or mentors. These individuals can assist in leading warm-ups, coordinating group activities, and providing support to their fellow teammates. 

Social Media Team: Social media is crucial for dance teams to showcase their talent, help with recruitment and engage with the community. It can feel daunting to handle it all as a coach. Members of the social media team can be tasked with content creation, scheduling posts, engagement and interaction.

Recruiting Team: Many coaches juggle additional responsibilities, which can limit their availability on campus to meet with potential dancers consistently. To address this challenge, the recruitment team steps in to meet with interested dancers, provide brief tours, offer guidance, and address any inquiries they may have. They can also help plan and assist recruiting camps and events. 

Appearance Request Team: Allows coaches to efficiently manage and coordinate appearance requests from external events, such as community performances, fundraisers, or promotional events. By delegating these tasks to a dedicated team, coaches can focus on their primary responsibilities.

Weight Room Leader: Having designated weight room leads empowers dancers to take ownership of their fitness goals and motivates them to lead by example. This delegation of responsibility fosters leadership skills and encourages teamwork as dancers collaborate to support each other's progress in the weight room.

Student Athlete Representative:  It provides a platform for the dance program to have a voice and presence within the broader athletic community, fostering recognition and respect for the team. This initiative strengthens the visibility and influence of the dance program while providing valuable leadership experience for the selected dancer.


Benefits of Delegation

Delegating tasks to dancers offers numerous benefits for both coaches and team members:

  1. Shared Responsibility: By involving dancers in various aspects of team management, you foster a sense of shared responsibility and ownership among team members.

  2. Skill Development: Delegating tasks provides dancers with opportunities to develop valuable skills such as leadership, communication, and organization. Additionally, they can build their resumes with these experiences, which will benefit them in the future.

  3. Time Management: By distributing tasks effectively, you can streamline workflow and allocate more time and energy to coaching and mentoring your team.

  4. Team Cohesion: Involving dancers in decision-making processes and collaborative projects strengthens bonds within the team and promotes a sense of unity and camaraderie.

Delegating tasks to dancers is a valuable strategy for promoting team involvement, reducing workload, and fostering a supportive and collaborative environment. By empowering dancers to take on responsibilities and contribute to the success of the team, coaches can cultivate a sense of ownership and shared accountability. As you navigate your coaching journey, consider the unique strengths and talents of your team members and leverage delegation as a tool for collective growth and achievement.

title: Planning and Filming Your Recruitment Video
content:
Creating a collegiate dance team recruitment video can be an exciting and daunting task and many do not know where to even start. A recruitment video provides the ability to showcase your talents, energy, and enthusiasm to join a particular program. In this blog post, we will give you quick tips and tricks to film, cut, and submit a video you feel confident about!

Planning Your Recruitment Video 


  1. Define Your Goals

The first step in creating a recruitment video is to define your goals. What teams are you trying to be recruited to? What style of dance do you want to compete in? Are you looking for a game day only school? Do you need to learn any new skills before filming? Once you know your goals, you can start funneling down the kind of content needed for your video. 



  1. Do Your Research 

Every collegiate dance team requires different skills, styles, and length of videos to be included in their recruitment submissions. All of this information can be located on their S2S profile or can usually be found on their teams website. If it is not listed, you can email the coach asking for details. 

  1. Showcase Recent Film

Coaches want to see film that are recent and highlights the level you are currently at. Do not submit film from a few years ago as it will give coaches a false impression. If you do not have any recent film due to an injury, communicate that with them directly. 



  1. Create a Storyboard

A storyboard is a visual representation of you and the contents of your video. It helps if you plan each shot and transition to ensure your video flows smoothly. Always open with an introduction and showcase your strongest styles and skills first! (unless directed otherwise) You want to grab their attention immediately!



  1. Write out an introduction 

Coaches want to know you as a dancer and a person. Use the introduction to vocalize your background, unique personal story and your interest in the program/university. Do not wing an introduction. When you put extra thought and effort into what you want to say, it shows! 



Filming Your Recruitment Video 


Once you have planned, it's time to start collecting and shooting footage! Here are some tips to help you create a high-quality video: 


  1. Use quality equipment 

You will want your video to be as professional-looking as possible and will require a camera, tripod, and a microphone. If you do not have access to professional equipment, you can use a smartphone camera and a stabilizer to capture stable shots. 



  1. No background distractions

Choose a location that is visually appealing where the lighting is good and there is no distracting background noises. Backdrop should be as minimalistic as possible, with no other dancers in the frame. 



  1. Record Good Audio 

Good audio is essential for a successful video. Make sure the audio is clear and not distorted. If you have background commentary in your video, edit it out or layer over a song of your choice. 



  1. Keep Shots Consistent 

When filming, do not transition back and forth from vertical to horizontal as it's distracting for coaches. You should be able to see the dancer the entire time, head to toe, and should not be following the dancer as they move throughout. 



  1. Dance harder than you think! 

Coaches want to see personality, energy and performance and it is your job to bring that to life coming from only a screen! Perform to the camera, make eye contact, and smile! Treat it just as you would for an in person audition, competition or performance.

title: Reflections of a Former Coach: Setbacks and Comebacks
content:
As I sit down to reflect on my time coaching at the University of Colorado, a whirlwind of memories and emotions flood through my mind. Five years have flown by, each season bringing its own challenges, triumphs, and most importantly, lessons. Now, as I embark on a new chapter in life, chasing the dream of entrepreneurship, I find myself filled with gratitude for the journey I've had and the incredible team that made it all worthwhile.

In the heat of the moment, coaching can feel like under appreciated work, but what I've learned over these past few weeks is that when you pour your heart and soul into something or someone, all that energy eventually comes flooding back to you. Now more than ever, I have felt the endless support from my athletes, fellow coaches, and the dance community. Although this change of leadership was abrupt and devastating, I've realized that all those years of sleepless nights, tough conversations, personal sacrifices, and behind-the-scenes efforts, have come back to me in such a beautiful and unexpected way. Coaching isn't about the trophies, status or ego. It's about fostering authentic relationships, empowering one another, and coming out on the other side as better humans. 

In my final season at CU, it wasn't the glitz and glam that stood out but rather the profound impact of the small things: the seniors' unwavering advocacy, Rylee's comforting hugs, Elizabeths encouraging texts, the sophomores' being my part-time dog sitters and the weird and goofy moments that would be incomprehensible to any outsider. My team cared for me as much as they cared for each other. Through the highs and lows of competition, the long practice hours, and moments of quiet support, we found strength in unity. Their support never failed to reignite my spark during moments when I felt my light dimming.


My dancers weren't just athletes I trained; they were family. 

As I turn the page to this next chapter, I am fueled by the fire and loyalty instilled in me by all of my dancers. The coaches, teachers, and mentors I've encountered along my journey have also shaped and inspired me. Studio 2 Stadium represents more than just a business venture; it's the culmination of my passion for dance, the knowledge I've gained, and my desire to give back. This platform is a tribute to everyone who has supported and believed in me, and it's my way of paying it forward and returning that positive energy.

As I say goodbye to the University of Colorado, I carry with me the love and appreciation of a coach whose life has been forever changed by the incredible individuals I've had the privilege to work with. To my team, past and present, thank you for the memories, the laughter, and the shared moments of growth. Here's to new beginnings and the endless possibilities that lie ahead. 

The comeback is always stronger than the setback.

As I prepare to embark on a new journey in entrepreneurship, I am filled with gratitude for the challenges, triumphs, and lessons that have shaped me. It’s a heartfelt tribute to my team, mentors, and the dance community, inspiring the transition to this next adventure in life.

title: Maximizing Your Performance at a Collegiate Football Game: Tips and Tricks for Looking and Feeling Your Best
content:
Before Kick Off

Prioritize Sleep by packing the night before: The night before the game, prioritize sleep to ensure you wake up feeling refreshed and energized. Aim for 7-9 hours of quality sleep to optimize your physical and mental performance on game day. If it's, an early morning kick off, pack uniforms, shower, and prepare breakfast the night before to help save time and stress!

Pre-Game IV Hydration: If budget allows, consider getting an IV infusion the day before the game to boost hydration levels and replenish electrolytes. This can help prevent dehydration and fatigue during the long day of activities. A cheaper option would be to drink gatorade, coconut water, and any other hydration supplements you prefer.

Skincare: Start your game day with a skincare routine that works best for you. As someone who has always struggled with acne, try to avoid pore clogging foundations and sunscreens that will irritate the skin further. You will be sweating the entire time so be smart about what makeup will best best for your skin type. Also apply sunscreen whenever you get the chance to protect your skin and avoid sunburns. You are outside for almost the entire day! 

Long-Lasting Makeup: Choose makeup products that are long-lasting and sweat-proof to withstand the rigors of game day. Opt for waterproof mascara, a matte foundation, and a lip stain that won't rub off during performances or cheering. Fake eyelashes are eye lash extensions are helpful in avoiding mascara smearing. 

Compression Socks: Wear compression socks to provide support and reduce fatigue, especially since you'll be standing or dancing for extended periods. Compression socks can also help improve circulation and prevent swelling in the legs and feet.

Chafing Prevention: Apply chafing cream to areas prone to irritation, such as the inner thighs and underarms, especially in hot weather. This will help prevent discomfort and chafing during performances or prolonged periods of activity.



During and After the Game

Eat Balanced Meals: Fuel your body with balanced meals that provide sustained energy throughout the day. Include complex carbohydrates, lean protein, and healthy fats in your pre-game meals to optimize performance and recovery.

Stay Hydrated: Drink plenty of water throughout the day to stay hydrated and maintain peak performance. Carry a water bottle with you and take sips regularly, especially during breaks in activities or performances.

Nutrient-Rich Snacks: Pack nutrient-rich snacks that are easy to eat on the go and provide the fuel your body needs. Opt for options like nuts, fruit, granola bars, sandwiches or protein shakes to keep energy levels up between meals.

Stay Fresh: After pregame events and during halftime you will have a few moments to freshen up before taking the field. Pack deodorant, body wipes, oil absorbing sheets, dry shampoo/hairspray and any other products for quick refreshment on hot days, so you can stay cool, comfortable, and confident no matter how high the temperatures!

By following these tips and tricks, you can ensure that you look and feel your best before performing at a collegiate football game. From prioritizing sleep and hydration to choosing long-lasting makeup and fueling your body with nutritious snacks, preparation is key to success on game day. Incorporate these strategies into your routine to maximize your performance and enjoy every moment of the experience.

title: The Importance of Feeling Good at an Audition: Focus on Your Dancing, Not Your Appearance
content:
The Power of Confidence
Confidence is a game-changer. When you feel good, it shows through in your performance. Judges and coaches can see your self-assurance, and it often translates into more dynamic and expressive dancing. Confidence helps you stay present, allowing you to focus on your technique, musicality, and stage presence.

One way to boost your confidence is by wearing clothes that make you feel great. The right outfit can make a significant difference in how you perceive yourself and, consequently, how you perform.

Choosing the Right Colors

Color psychology plays a vital role in how we feel. Wearing colors that you love and that make you feel powerful can enhance your mood and self-assurance. Here are some tips on choosing the right colors for your audition:

  • Bold and Bright: Colors like red, yellow, and orange can make you feel energetic and vibrant. These colors draw attention and can help you stand out.

  • Cool and Calm: Shades like blue, green, and purple can have a calming effect, helping you stay composed and focused.

  • Neutrals and Classics: Black, white, and gray are timeless and can make you feel polished and professional. They also serve as great bases for adding pops of color with accessories.

School Colors vs. Personal Preference

While wearing school colors can show your spirit and dedication, it's not always necessary unless specified in the audition guidelines. If you feel more confident in other colors, go for it! The key is to choose an outfit that makes you feel your best. Your confidence and comfort will shine through far more than adhering strictly to a color scheme.

Remember, the judges are looking at your talent and how you carry yourself. If you feel great in what you're wearing, it will reflect in your performance.

Practical Tips for Audition Attire

Here are some practical tips for choosing your audition outfit:

  • Comfort is Key: Make sure your outfit allows for full range of motion. Avoid anything too tight or restrictive.

  • Fit and Function: Choose clothes that fit well and stay in place while you dance. You don’t want to be adjusting your outfit mid-performance.

  • Personal Touch: Add a personal touch to your outfit, whether it's a unique accessory or a favorite piece of clothing that makes you feel special.

  • Practice Run: Wear your audition outfit during a practice session to ensure it feels good and works well for your routine.

  • Bring Backup Safety Pins: You never know if you might have a wardrobe malfunction, your audition number isn't staying on, or you might need extra support after your outfit gets sweaty. Always come over prepared!

title: Navigating a Collegiate Recruitment Clinic: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Preparing for the Clinic


Research the Program: Begin by researching the dance team program you are interested in. Understand their style, expectations, and any specific requirements they may have. This knowledge will help you tailor your preparation accordingly.


Physical Conditioning: Ensure that you are in good physical shape by engaging in regular exercise and conditioning routines. Strengthening your technique, flexibility, and stamina will enhance your performance during the clinic.


Understand the team style: Familiarize yourself with the team's game day routines, competition pieces and choreography style. Study their quality of movement and performance expectations both on the field and on the stage. 


What to Expect at the Clinic


Check-In: Arrive at the clinic early to give yourself plenty of time to find parking, check in and warm up. Most coaches will send a schedule prior to the clinic with details in regards to clinic structure and expectations. If they do not specify prior, come wearing something you feel confident and can easily move in a color that makes you stand out.  


Technique Classes: Expect to participate in technique classes relevant to the team's style. They will most likely have dancers go across the floor or stay center floor to assess skill level. Be attentive, show your best effort, and ask questions if needed. Expect various turns, leaps, legs/flexibility and acrobatics to be in your combinations. 


Choreography Sessions: You will likely learn choreography during the clinic. The team's choreographer, coach or a current team member will teach routines. Stand in a position where you can see the choreographer but still have room to dance full out. 


Quick tip: Always dance full out unless told otherwise. It will not only help you grasp the choreography quicker but will give coaches more opportunity to watch you dance, while learning. 


Individual Auditions: Be prepared for individual auditions, where you may perform a solo or be asked to improv across the floor. This is your chance to stand out and showcase your unique abilities, any skills or styles that you are confident in and prove to coaches why you would be a great fit for their program. 


Quick tip: Never throw a skill that you have not executed correctly before. Today is not the day to experiment!


Maximizing Your Experience


Professionalism: Maintain a positive and professional attitude throughout the clinic. Show respect towards coaches, team members, and other participants. Remember, your behavior both on and off the dance floor will be observed and considered. Be friendly and smile! 


Active Listening and Feedback: Pay close attention to instructions, corrections, and feedback given by the coaches and team members. Showcase your adaptability but do not be afraid to ask questions. Majority of coaches want to interact with prospects and can not read your mind if you are confused or need clarification.


Building Relationships: Relationships are key when it comes to recruitment! Take advantage of the opportunity to network and connect with current team members, coaches, and other dancers. Engage in conversations, ask questions, and express your genuine interest in the program. Know that dancers will always talk to coaches following a recruitment clinic to give them insight to their experience with prospects; create positive interactions! 


Be yourself: While technical skills are crucial, don't forget to let your personality shine. Collegiate teams require so much more from a dancer outside of their abilities. Coaches are looking for dancers that align with their team culture, coaching styles, and campus community. Bring your unique style and energy and enjoy the journey!


Follow up: Email coaches prior to attending their camp thanking them for their time. You will want to remind the coach of your name, where you are from, what number you were and what you were wearing. Coaches have to watch so many dancers in a short amount of time that they will want details in your follow up to easily reference their notes. 


Attending a dance team collegiate recruitment clinic can be a thrilling and nerve-wracking experience. By adequately preparing, understanding what to expect, and maximizing your experience, you can significantly increase your chances of catching the attention of coaches and earning a coveted spot on a collegiate dance team.

title: Recovery: The Key to Sustaining a Long Dance Career.
content:
In the past, dancers lived by the mantra “practice makes perfect”. Ingrained into their everyday vocabulary both on and off the stage. Training, going across the floor over and over and over until they would perfect a certain skill. Spending countless hours at the studio, limiting their time for studies, friends, social events and family bonding. Harnessing their skill set, mastering various styles and pushing their physical and mental limits to the max in hopes to see instant improvement. Mentally spiraling telling themselves “I am not enough. I need to do more”. Dancers possess an incredible amount of dedication to their training, pushing their limits everytime they are in the studio. 



However, amidst the rigorous training, rehearsals, and performances, it is crucial to prioritize recovery. Recovery allows dancers to rejuvenate their bodies, prevent injuries, and maintain their mental well-being. If dancers prioritize recovery, and treat it just as importantly as their training, they will sustain their dance careers both physically and mentally. 



The Physical Benefits of Recovery



Restoring Muscular Strength and Endurance

Intense dance training can lead to muscular fatigue and breakdown. Adequate recovery time allows the muscles to repair and rebuild, enhancing strength and endurance. We'll discuss the importance of incorporating rest days, proper sleep, and nutrition to optimize physical recovery.



Preventing Injuries

Overuse injuries are common among dancers. Recovery periods provide an opportunity to identify and address any potential issues before they escalate. We'll explore techniques such as stretching, foam rolling, and cross-training to minimize the risk of injuries and maintain peak physical condition.



Promotes Mental Health

Dance is not just a physically demanding art form; it also requires immense mental focus. Continuous training and performing can lead to performance anxiety and mental exhaustion. Its key is to incorporate recovery practices, such as meditation, breathing exercises, and mindfulness, to help dancers manage anxiety and cultivate a positive mindset.



Recovery Tools

While physical recovery is crucial for dancers, it's important to acknowledge that it can also come with a financial cost. The expenses associated with recovery methods and practices can vary depending on individual needs and preferences. title: Loss, Love, and the Power of Dance to Heal
content:
This week's blog isn't about tips, insider information, audition attire, or anything directly related to dance teams. Instead, it's something personal to me, and if it connects with even one person, then I'll feel like I've shared something worthwhile.


On September 5th, my partner Danny and I returned from a quick grocery run to find my dog Gunnar had passed away in a tragic accident. The pain was, and still is, immense. Yet, even in this darkness, I find myself filled with gratitude for the time we had with him and the incredible community that loved him.


For those who knew me, Gunnar was an inseparable part of my life. We were a package deal. He was my constant companion, always by my side as we traveled and explored together. From hitting the mountain trails to bombing down snowy slopes, cruising on long road trips, or swimming in any lake or river he could find - that goofball was always up for the adventure. His presence was a given in all aspects of my life, including at the dance studio. 


Gunnar was more than just my pet; he was a cherished member of my dance family. His excited barks greeting everyone at the door, his playful presence during warm-ups, clever maneuvers for snacks and even his afternoon naps in the teacher's lounge were all part of our daily routine. He brought joy, comfort, and often comic relief during stressful times. The love he received from my dancers was truly special.


In this time of loss, I've found solace in an unexpected place - the dance studio. While returning to work has been challenging, stepping back into the studio feels like coming home. Being surrounded by the people who bring me as much joy as Gunnar once did, has been a source of comfort and healing.


Dance, like Gunnar, has always been my constant. It's been there to provide light in dark times, understanding in confusion, and unconditional love in pain. I'm profoundly grateful for this art form and the community it has given me. Dance, much like the love we have for our pets, is something we pour our hearts into, knowing that at some point, transitions and goodbyes are inevitable.


Whether you're still actively dancing, coaching, or have moved on to other pursuits, I hope you can reflect on the dance community with gratitude. We're fortunate to be part of a craft and a family that not only challenges us to grow but also helps us heal in times of need.
description: This week’s blog is a personal reflection on finding comfort in unexpected places. I hope it resonates with anyone who has experienced loss or is seeking solace in their own way.

title: Why Ballet Matters: The Unseen Power Behind Collegiate Dance Success
content:
As a dance teacher and coach, one of the most common challenges I see with high school dancers looking to continue their dance careers in college is a lack of consistent, high-quality ballet training. While many aspiring collegiate dancers may prefer other styles like jazz, contemporary, or hip hop, the reality is that a strong foundation in classical ballet technique is absolutely essential to succeed at the next level.

The precise body alignment, core strength, and spatial awareness developed through ballet classes are the building blocks that allow dancers to pick up choreography quickly, execute complex movements with control and articulation, and maintain proper technique.

Coaches and directors at the collegiate level can immediately spot dancers who have been consistently taking ballet class. Their lines are longer, their turns are cleaner, and their overall confidence in their dancing is noticeable. It's not that they are innately "better" dancers - it's that the hours and years they've spent perfecting their ballet technique have given them the tools to pick up and excel at any style they're asked to perform.

Pushing Through the Discomfort of Ballet Training

I know it can be tempting for young dancers to want to focus only on the styles they enjoy the most. If you're a hip hop fanatic, the last thing you may want to do is go to yet another ballet barre. And if contemporary or modern is your jam, the rigidity and structure of ballet class might not seem very appealing. But I can say with certainty that the dancers who push through and make ballet a priority in their training regimen are the ones who tend to have the smoothest transitions to the college dance world.

The skills and habits cultivated in ballet class - the attention to detail, the discipline to keep working at something even when it's challenging, the body awareness and control - are invaluable assets no matter what style of dance you want to pursue. Even if ballet is not your favorite, treating it as an essential part of your training will pay dividends down the line. The confidence, versatility, and technical mastery you build will set you apart when auditioning for college dance programs.

The Long-Term Benefits of Ballet

At the end of the day, dance is a highly demanding field that requires incredible commitment, resilience, and attention to detail. Collegiate dance programs are extremely competitive, with talented dancers competing for a limited number of spots. Having a rock-solid ballet foundation is one of the best ways to position yourself for success.

It may not always be easy or fun, but making ballet a consistent part of your training regimen will give you the tools to thrive not just in college, but in the professional dance world beyond. The confidence that comes from years of ballet training are an invaluable asset that will serve you well, no matter what your ultimate dance goals may be. So stick with it, trust the process, and watch as your dancing reaches new heights!

title: Team Bonding: Understanding Its Significance and Integrating It into Regular Practice
content:
Three crucial elements contribute significantly to team bonding: establishing trust, effective communication, and promoting unity.

In dance, trust is indispensable. Whether its taking the floor with your team, cleaning a section, drilling your turns, or executing intricate lifts, dancers must have implicit trust in each other's abilities. Team bonding activities create a foundation of trust by fostering understanding and camaraderie among team members.

Effective communication is the backbone of any successful dance routine. Team bonding exercises encourage open dialogue and active listening, allowing dancers to better convey ideas, provide constructive feedback, and support each other on and off the stage.

A dance team is a cohesive unit, and unity among its members is crucial for achieving collective goals. Through team bonding activities, dancers develop a sense of belonging and solidarity, leading to a stronger, more unified team dynamic.

Integrating Team Bonding into Practice

Silly Games and Activities: This does not have to happen every practice, as we know there are always time constraints. However from time to time, kick off practice sessions with fun activities to loosen up the atmosphere and encourage interaction among team members. This could include games like Two Truths and a Lie, Human Knot, and my personal favorite Just Dance. Just Dance is not only a great way to laugh but serves as a fun and different cardio warm up!

Collaborative Choreography Sessions: Allocate time for collaborative choreography sessions where dancers work together to create new routines. This not only fosters creativity but also encourages teamwork and cooperation as dancers collaborate to bring their collective vision to life.

Goal Setting:Incorporating goal setting into practice sessions is a pivotal aspect of integrating team bonding. By collectively setting goals, dancers not only align their aspirations but also foster a sense of shared purpose and commitment within the team. You can write daily goals, word of the day, and long term goals on the mirrors to keep dancers focused and motivated.

Appreciation Activity: Periodically, I would engage my team in this exercise, which serves to make dancers feel acknowledged and cherished by their peers. Each dancer starts with a piece of paper, writing their name at the top. Then, we pass the papers clockwise, allowing each team member to express their gratitude towards the dancer named on the paper. By the end, the dancer will have received notes from every teammate, serving as a powerful reminder of their value and the commitment shared within the team.

Establishing Rituals: Incorporate team rituals into your practice routine, such as pre-performance playlists, post-practice reflections, meditation, etc. These rituals serve as anchor points for team members, fostering a sense of continuity and shared experience. When dancers know what to expect, it helps them feel more in control and connected to their peers. 

Encouraging Peer Support: Create opportunities for peer mentoring and support within the team. Pair experienced dancers with newcomers or assign buddy systems to ensure that every member feels supported and valued. 

Celebrating the Small Wins: Acknowledge and celebrate milestones together, whether it's a successful performance, a breakthrough in choreography, or personal achievements of team members. Recognizing accomplishments reinforces team spirit and motivates dancers to continue striving for excellence.

In the world of dance, the bonds forged between team members are as essential as the steps they perform. By prioritizing team bonding and integrating it into regular practice, dance teams can cultivate a supportive and cohesive environment where each member feels valued, inspired, and empowered to reach their full potential. Ultimately, it is these strong connections that elevate a group of dancers from mere performers to a unified and extraordinary team.

title: Beyond High School: Preparing Your Dancer for Success
content:
As a high school dance coach, you play a crucial role in shaping young dancers' futures, many of whom aspire to dance at the collegiate level. This journey is rewarding but highly competitive. Studio 2 Stadium offers essential guidance, allowing you to focus on coaching without spending hours navigating the collegiate dance landscape. This blog provides a brief overview of key elements in this process, and we’re dedicated to offering professional insights to support your dancers' success. We encourage you to get your dancers onto our platform for valuable resources tailored to their aspirations.

Understanding the Dance Team Landscape

College dance teams can fall under various umbrellas within a university, which will impact the structure, resources, and expectations of the team. Here are the most common categories:

  • Athletic Department: These teams are often considered varsity sports and benefit from funding, scholarships, and support services from the athletic department.

  • Club Sports: Dance teams under club sports have more autonomy but fewer institutional resources. They may rely on membership fees and fundraising.

  • Marching Band: Some universities integrate dance teams with their marching band, offering additional performance opportunities.

  • Student Activities/Marketing: Dance teams may also be recognized as student organizations or may fall under the university’s marketing or event-planning departments.

    Coaching Structure: Teams may also vary in their coaching setup. Some have a dedicated head coach, while others are overseen by an advisor who manages the entire spirit program, including cheer and mascots. In some cases, teams may even be self-coached, which can provide more flexibility but requires strong leadership within the team.

    NIL Opportunities: The ability for dancers to profit from NIL (Name, Image, Likeness) deals is expanding. Dancers can now secure sponsorships, brand endorsements, and promotional opportunities, just like athletes in other sports. NIL deals can include partnerships with local businesses, social media influencer opportunities, and collaborations with national brands, allowing dancers to monetize their personal brand while still competing. This growing area is especially relevant for dancers who maintain a strong online presence, offering a new revenue stream while pursuing their college careers.

    Game Day Responsibilities: College dance teams often perform at various sporting events, requiring them to engage with the crowd through halftime shows, sideline performances, and fan interactions. These responsibilities can lead to significant time commitments, including travel for away games and the more sports a team covers, the more time one has to dedicate.

    Competition vs. Performance-Based Teams: Some dance teams focus solely on performances (e.g., halftime shows), while others compete in national competitions like UDA, NDA or DTU. Performance-based teams often focus more on crowd engagement, while competitive teams emphasize technique training, athleticism, and stamina.




Understanding the Recruitment Process

The recruitment process for college dance teams can vary significantly between schools. However, there are some common elements that your dancers should be aware of:

  • Timing and Deadlines: Many teams require video auditions to be submitted during the fall semester. Remind your dancers to stay on top of these deadlines well in advance.

  • Audition Requirements: These may include technical demonstrations, performance choreography, or even interviews. Ensure your dancers research the specifics for each team.

  • Scholarship Opportunities: Not all teams offer financial support, but some do. Encourage your dancers to inquire early about scholarship availability and processes.

  • Time Commitments: College dance team schedules can be rigorous. Dancers should assess how they will manage both their academic workload and dance team responsibilities.

  • Academic Standards: Many teams have minimum GPA requirements, so it’s essential for your dancers to maintain academic excellence.




Preparing for Dance Team Auditions

Preparation is key to successful auditions, and as a coach, you can help your dancers master these essential skills:

  • Technical Proficiency: Ensure they are well-versed in a wide range of dance styles and techniques.

  • Performance Quality: Encourage strong showmanship and the ability to quickly learn and execute choreography.

  • Audition Readiness: Help them practice learning choreography quickly and performing in a high-pressure environment.

  • Developing Interpersonal Skills: As a representative of both the team and the university, it’s crucial to practice strong interpersonal skills.

  • Academic Standing: Reinforce the need to maintain strong grades, as academic performance often plays a role in eligibility.


Having Realistic Conversations with Dancers

As a coach, one of your most challenging but essential responsibilities is managing the expectations of your dancers and their families. Here's how to approach these difficult conversations:

Setting Realistic Goals

Assess your dancers' current skills and potential, and help them set achievable goals for their college dance aspirations. Avoid inflating their expectations, as this can lead to disappointment.

Discussing Alternative Paths

If a dancer's dream of a prestigious dance program is unlikely to be realized, present them with other viable options, such as BA programs, dance minors, or club teams. Emphasize that there are many ways to continue dancing in college.

Addressing Injuries and Limitations

Ask your dancer, “If you were injured today and couldn’t dance, where would you want to go to school?” This question encourages them to consider their college choice beyond dance. If your dancer is facing physical limitations or recovering from an injury, have an open discussion about how it could affect their dance opportunities in college. Provide support and guidance to help them manage their condition while adjusting their goals for the future.

Providing Unbiased Advice

As a coach, it's crucial that you remain objective and provide your dancers with honest, unbiased feedback. This may sometimes mean delivering news that is difficult to hear, but it's essential for their long-term success.

Guiding high school dancers towards their college dance aspirations is a rewarding yet challenging responsibility. By understanding the college dance landscape, preparing your dancers for auditions, managing expectations, and building a support network, you can help them navigate this pivotal transition. Remember, your role as a coach extends far beyond the studio walls - you are a critical partner in shaping their future success.

title: Why Mixing It Up Matters: Building Confidence Through Diverse Dance Training
content:
When you train with different teachers and experience various dance styles, you develop a crucial skill: adaptability. This flexibility in your approach to movement and learning makes you more prepared for whatever a prospect clinic might throw your way. Think about it – every choreographer has their unique style and way of teaching. By exposing yourself to multiple teaching methods and dance styles, you're essentially preparing yourself for the unexpected.

Breaking Out of Your Comfort Zone

It's natural to feel comfortable with your regular dance instructor. They understand your strengths, weaknesses, and learning style, and over time, you've built a strong sense of trust with them. However, limiting yourself to one teaching style can actually hinder your growth. Here's why stepping out of your comfort zone matters:

  1. Different perspectives on technique

  2. Exposure to diverse teaching methods

  3. Building resilience and adaptability

  4. Expanding your dance vocabulary

Making Connections in a Small World

The dance community, despite seeming vast, is surprisingly interconnected. Every new class, workshop, or studio you visit is an opportunity to:

  • Network with fellow dancers

  • Learn from experienced professionals

  • Build relationships with potential mentors

  • Create connections that could lead to future opportunities

Finding Your "Aha!" Moments

Every teacher has their unique way of explaining concepts and techniques. What might be unclear when explained one way could become crystal clear when presented differently. By exposing yourself to various teaching styles, you increase your chances of experiencing those lightbulb moments where everything just clicks.

Imagine struggling with a particular turn sequence. Your regular teacher might focus on spotting technique, but another instructor might approach it from a grounding perspective. Suddenly, that challenging combination becomes manageable because you've gained a new understanding of the mechanics.

Don't Pigeon-Hole Yourself

Versatility is increasingly valued in the dance world. By diversifying your training, you:

  • Become more well-rounded as a dancer

  • Increase your marketability

  • Develop a unique style that incorporates various influences

  • Build confidence in your ability to handle different situations

Tips for Expanding Your Dance Training

  1. Research local studios and try classes with different instructors

  2. Attend workshops and conventions to experience intensive training in various styles

  3. Follow dancers and choreographers on social media to learn about training opportunities

  4. Be open to feedback from all instructors – each perspective adds value

  5. Keep a dance journal to track your progress and “ah-ha” moments from different classes

Remember, the goal isn't to replace your primary training but to complement it. Your regular classes provide the foundation, while diverse experiences build upon that base to create a more confident, adaptable, and skilled dancer. As you prepare for prospect clinics, embrace the opportunity to learn from as many teachers as possible. Not only will this build your confidence, but it will also make you a more versatile and connected dancer in an industry where adaptability and relationships matter just as much as technique.

So go ahead – take that class at the new studio, sign up for that workshop with the guest choreographer, and embrace the beautiful diversity of the dance world. Your future self will thank you for it.

title: Connecting Through the Camera: Making a Memorable Intro for Your Recruitment Video
content:
Setting the Scene

Before you hit record, ensure your setup is professional:

  • Position your camera at eye level (ring lights are always a great option for stable leveling)

  • Find a quiet space with a clean, uncluttered background

Appearance

  • Keep hair neat and professional

  • Apply natural-looking makeup that will show well on camera

Content Structure

Start with a warm, natural greeting. Rather than memorizing lines, keep these key points in mind to discuss organically:

  1. Personal Introduction

    • Share your name with a genuine smile

    • Mention your hometown, but make it personal ("I grew up dancing in [city]...")

    • Connect your background to why you're interested in their program

    • Make it conversational,, inviting and don't be afraid to use your hands while speaking

  2. Dance Background

    • Briefly share your journey chronologically, but focus on meaningful moments

    • Highlight experiences that align with the university's values

    • Mention specific achievements without sounding like you're reading a resume

  3. Program Connection

    • Reference specific aspects of their dance program that excite you

    • Connect your goals with what their program and University offers


Speaking Tips

DO:

  • Take brief pauses between thoughts- you can always go back and edit@

  • Use natural hand gestures

  • Maintain eye contact with the camera

  • Show enthusiasm through vocal variation

  • Share specific stories that demonstrate your personality

AVOID:

  • Reading from notes

  • Speaking too quickly

  • Using filler words repeatedly

  • Reciting achievements like a list

  • Over-rehearsing (which can sound robotic)


Example Flow

Here's how you might naturally connect these elements:

"Hi! I’m Sarah, and I’m thrilled to share why [University Name]’s dance team feels like the perfect next step for me! I started dancing at age six in my hometown of [City], but my passion for this university really took off when I attended my first football game at 10 years old with my dad. I didn't watch a single moment of the game; I was entranced by the dancers on the sidelines and vividly remember telling my dad, ‘I want to be just like them when I’m older!’ That experience sparked a fire in me, and ever since, I’ve dreamed of joining this team and sharing my love for dance with others in such an exciting atmosphere!"


Final Tips

  • Record a test video to check your lighting, sound, and energy

  • Practice your key points but don't memorize exact words

  • Be yourself – programs want to see your authentic personality

  • Share specific examples of why their program stands out to you

  • Remember to smile and let your personality show!
